newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage-takers agree to talks with government.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage-takers agree to talks with government.

text.p: Peruvian Marxist rebels holding 72 VIP captives in Lima confirmed on Monday they were willing to restart face-to-face talks with the government aimed at negotiating a solution to the 55-day hostage siege.

But the rebels said they would not drop their main demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades in the talks set for Tuesday and accused Peru's President Alberto Fujimori of making a "veiled threat" to use force against them.

In a reminder of the high stakes at the siege site, an explosion was heard in the afternoon at the back of the compound, followed by several rounds of gunfire from the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.

"It's still not certain but it seems to have been at the back of the residence in the garden. The terrorists had mined the area and it seems that some animal -- a cat -- activated (the device)," a policeman said. He said the shots were "a reaction of the terrorists thinking someone was entering."
A Red Cross official confirmed there were no injuries.

Earlier, in a statement via walkie-talkie from inside the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence, rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini said the MRTA "manifests its total willingness to start conversations (with the government) on Tuesday."

He added that the MRTA had always been willing to hold talks but would not relinquish its "unrevocable" position. "The beginning of the talks does not necessarily mean the beginning of the solution to the conflict," he warned.

Fujimori has ruled out considering the release of MRTA prisoners, and this had stalled previous attempts to restart negotiations. Fujimori has also ruled out paying ransom money, although he has floated the possibility of allowing the MRTA rebels to take asylum abroad.

Cerpa accused Fujimori of making statements during his current visit to London "that if the conversations fail, it would be a step towards the use of force." This, he said, "constitutes a veiled threat, trying to turn it at the same time into a psyschological weapon."

The president announced on Sunday that conversations were set to resume on Tuesday between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and Cerpa's deputy, Roli Rojas, known by his nom de guerre "El Arabe" -- The Arab.

Rojas, a 34-year-old former bus fare collector, joined the MRTA while a university student, police sources said. He was jailed in 1986 but escaped in 1990 and rose rapidly through MRTA ranks to his current position as Cerpa's right-hand man.
Fujimori described the imminent conversations as "preliminary talks" intended to pave the way for "definitive talks, probably with Cerpa Cartolini himself."
In the only previous face-to-face contact, Palermo met Cerpa in late December inside the diplomatic residence that the MRTA stormed during a cocktail party on Dec. 17.
In the walkie-talkie conversation, Cerpa said the rebels were as "determined to face a peaceful or military solution with the same conviction" as they had started the siege.

Officials and mediators finalised logistics on Monday for the talks. As police widened the security zone around a private house opposite the residence selected for the meeting, Red Cross officials took charge of furnishing the interior.

Rojas was to be transported to the house in a bullet-proof van. No weapons will be allowed inside because the house will be under Red Cross jurisdiction. A peace talks commission representing the Vatican, Canadian government and Red Cross will oversee the talks, where Tokyo will have an observer.

Police outside the compound, which the MRTA has mined and booby-trapped, kept up their psychological warfare on Monday, blaring traditional patriotic "criollo" music over loudspeakers aimed at the building. The MRTA also began the day with its now routine broadcast of a revolutionary anthem in honour of fallen comrades, followed by shouted slogans.

The roughly 15 rebels' hostages include Fujimori's brother Pedro, two government ministers, the ambassadors of Bolivia and Japan, a handful of top security force and judiciary officials and two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
